h1: The 8 Best Glass Desktop Whiteboards of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best Glass Desktop Whiteboards: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: eight glass desktop whiteboards from Quartet and others, compared on size, storage and keyboard-stand design.
summary: The Quartet GDP1723W is the best overall, with a 17 by 23 inch magnetic glass panel, trays and magnets. The TSJ OFFICE doubles as a keyboard stand with a drawer, and the Quartet GDP186 is a slim 18 by 6 inch strip for monitor-side notes. The calculator board, the GDE119 pad, the grey drawer stand, the wood-stand mini and the 8 by 6 inch board cover narrower needs.
intro: Most people buy a desktop whiteboard the way they buy a coaster: small, cheap and quickly regretted. The writing area is what you are actually paying for, and an 8 by 6 inch slab holds one short list before you start erasing. Frame, finish and brand come second. A glass surface also wipes cleaner than a laminate one, which is why these boards exist at all.

Our editors reviewed eight glass desktop boards and ranked them on writing area, storage, what ships in the box and how much desk each one claims. Scores follow the listings. Where a board's dimensions are not stated, that gap counts against it, because a surface you cannot measure is a surface you cannot plan around.

products.name: Quartet Glass Whiteboard Desktop Panel, Magnetic, 17"x23", Dry Erase, with Accessory Trays and Magnets (GDP1723W)
products.verdict: The largest writing area here, with magnets and trays to match.
products.description:
The GDP1723W is a 17 by 23 inch glass panel with a magnetic surface, magnets and accessory trays. That is the biggest writing area in the ranking, and the only board here you can pin notes to with magnets. A single marker comes in the listing, and trays hold spares, so the desk stays tidy.

It wins because it offers the most space, the only magnetic surface and the Quartet name. Against everything below it, the tradeoff is price: it is the only board in the $100 to $200 bucket.

Buy it if you plan, sketch or manage a project from your desk. The caveat: a 17 by 23 inch panel claims real desk depth, so measure before you order. On a narrow desk it will sit awkwardly beside a monitor and keyboard.
products.idealFor: Planners who want a full-size glass board beside the monitor.
products.skipIf: Your desk has little spare room.

products.name: TSJ OFFICE Small Desktop Whiteboard, Glass Dry Erase Board, Computer Keyboard Stand with Drawer
products.verdict: A keyboard stand, drawer and whiteboard in one footprint.
products.description:
The TSJ OFFICE gets two jobs from one footprint: a glass dry erase surface that doubles as a keyboard stand, with a built-in storage drawer underneath. Raising the keyboard frees desk area, and the drawer swallows markers, sticky notes and a charging cable.

It ranks second because it solves the small-desk problem. Compared with the Quartet GDP1723W it has no magnetic surface or trays, but it costs far less, in the $25 to $50 bucket, and hides small items. Against the grey stand, it carries the stronger brand.

Choose it for crowded desks where storage and a board both matter. The caveats are that the listing does not state the writing size, and your keyboard needs to fit the stand. Measure the keyboard first.
products.idealFor: Small desks that need storage and a board.
products.skipIf: You want a large writing area.

products.name: Quartet Glass Dry Erase White Board, Desktop Computer Pad for Notetaking, 18"x6" with Storage (GDP186)
products.verdict: A wide, shallow strip that fits in front of a monitor.
products.description:
The GDP186 is an 18 by 6 inch glass pad with storage and one marker. Its shape is the point: wide and shallow, it sits in front of a monitor or tucked against the keyboard, holding a to-do list or reminders where your eyes already are.

It lands third because 6 inches of height suits notes and reminders but not diagrams or sketches. Against the TSJ it gives up the keyboard-stand function, and against the 9 by 11 pad below it offers a wider surface in return for less depth.

It suits people who jot lists all day and want them in view. The caveat: the listing does not describe a magnetic surface, so you cannot pin anything to it, and six inches fills up fast with more than a handful of lines.
products.idealFor: Notes and lists in front of a monitor.

products.name: Small Glass Desktop Whiteboard Dry Erase Board with Calculator, Keyboard Stand Organizer
products.verdict: A keyboard-stand board with a calculator built in.
products.description:
This keyboard-stand board adds a calculator to a glass dry erase surface. The listing says markers and an eraser come in the box, and it works as a keyboard stand organizer. The calculator keeps sums on the desk, not on a phone.

It ranks below the TSJ because the calculator is the main extra rather than a storage drawer, and the listing states no dimensions. For number-heavy desk work, that is a fair swap, and it costs about the same, in the $25 to $50 bucket.

Choose it if you add figures all day, in accounts or invoices, and want one device on the desk. The caveats are that the size is not stated, and there is no drawer for markers. Confirm the dimensions with the seller before you commit.
products.idealFor: Desk workers who do quick sums.
products.skipIf: You want storage over a calculator.

products.name: Quartet Dry Erase White Board 9"W x 11"H Desktop Glass Pad with Removable Clip and Marker (GDE119)
products.verdict: A letter-sized glass pad with a clip for paper.
products.description:
The GDE119 is a 9 by 11 inch glass pad, close to letter size, with a removable paper clip and a marker. The clip is the touch that sets it apart: it lets you hold a printed page next to your notes, which suits transcription and checklists.

It ranks fifth because it is a plain pad with no storage and no stand function. Against the slim GDP186 it offers more height, but less width, and it costs the same, $25 to $50.

Buy it if you want a simple, familiar pad for daily notes and occasional diagrams. The caveats are no storage and no stand, so markers wander across the desk. If you want accessories managed, move up to the TSJ.
products.idealFor: A simple pad for daily notes.

products.name: Small Desktop Glass Whiteboard Dry-Erase Board, Computer Keyboard Stand with Drawer
products.verdict: Same keyboard-stand-with-drawer idea, with a grey finish option.
products.description:
This small glass board is a keyboard stand with a built-in drawer and a glass dry erase surface, with a grey finish option. The format matches the TSJ: raise the keyboard, write on the glass, tuck the clutter inside.

It ranks sixth because it offers the same idea without the same brand recognition, and the listing is thin on detail. The grey finish is the real differentiator, useful if your desk setup is grey or monochrome.

Pick it if finish matters and you want the stand and drawer in a muted colour. The caveats are the unstated size and the sparse listing. Ask the seller for the writing area and the dimensions of the stand before you order, and compare with the TSJ at a similar price.
products.idealFor: Buyers matching a grey desk setup.

products.name: Desktop Black Glass Dry Erase Whiteboard with Reversible Wood Stand, Small (9.5"x6.7")
products.verdict: A tiny black glass board on a reversible wood stand.
products.description:
This is a 9.5 by 6.7 inch black glass dry erase board on a reversible wood stand, with a marker and eraser included. The stand flips to hold the board in either orientation, which suits a minimalist desk, and the black glass reads as a design object.

It ranks seventh because the writing area is small. It beats the 8 by 6 inch mini on stand design and size, but it is not meant for more than a list. The under $25 price reflects that.

It suits desks that favour a neat look and short notes. The caveat: the small surface limits what you can write, and a black surface needs the right marker, so check what the listing supplies. For real planning, choose one of the larger boards.

products.name: Black Mini Desktop Pure Glass Whiteboard, Small Glass Dry-Erase Whiteboard, 8"x6" with 5 markers
products.verdict: The cheapest way to try a glass board, with five markers.
products.description:
The mini is 8 by 6 inches of black pure glass with five markers listed. It has the lowest price in the guide, under $25, and the tiny footprint barely registers on a desk.

It ranks last because it offers the smallest writing area and no stand or storage. What it gives you is the lowest cost of entry and a generous marker count, which is why it works as a trial.

Buy it as a low-risk first glass board, to see whether you will use one. The caveat: at 8 by 6 inches it holds a handful of lines, and you will quickly outgrow it. If the habit sticks, step up to the GDE119 or GDP186.

whatMatters.detail: Writing area is the usable glass surface in inches. It decides whether the board holds a list or a plan. Look for exact dimensions in the title and bullets, not just the words small or large, and compare them with your desk depth and your monitor stand. Several listings here do not state a size, which is a reason to ask.

Some boards double as a stand that lifts the keyboard and adds a surface. That saves desk space but ties the board to your keyboard position. Check the listing for the words keyboard stand, and confirm your keyboard fits, since listings often omit the stand's width. A tall stand can also strain wrists if it lifts the keyboard too high.

A magnetic glass board lets you pin notes with magnets, which turns it into a small planning wall. Only the Quartet GDP1723W lists magnets here. If you pin reminders, look for the word magnetic and confirm that magnets are included, since some boards are glass only and magnets will slide off. Stronger magnets hold more paper.

A drawer or tray keeps markers and clips from spreading across the desk, which matters on small desks. Check whether storage is built in or sold separately, and how deep it is. The TSJ and the grey stand include a drawer, and the GDP1723W adds trays. A pad with no storage needs a pen cup, which takes up the space you saved.

A board with no marker is unusable on arrival. Counts range from one to five on these listings. Confirm what the listing says is in the box, including an eraser, and check whether the black boards expect a particular marker colour. Spare markers are cheap, but a dry marker on day one is annoying.

faq.a: Several do. The mini lists five, the GDE119 and GDP186 list one each, and the GDP1723W lists one. Check the box contents on the page before buying, and note that marker quality varies.

faq.q: Is glass better than a plastic board?
faq.a: Glass is generally smoother to wipe. The listings describe glass surfaces, but they do not give ghosting data, so rely on the surface description alone and wipe promptly, before ink has time to set.

faq.q: Will a keyboard-stand board fit my keyboard?
faq.a: The listings do not give full dimensions, so measure your keyboard and compare it with the dimensions on the product page. The TSJ and the grey stand are the likely fits, but only the seller can confirm.

faq.q: Is a black glass board harder to use?
faq.a: Not necessarily. The two black boards list markers or an eraser in the box. Confirm which marker type each expects before you buy, since a black surface needs a bold, light-coloured marker, not a standard dark one.

faq.q: Is the 17 by 23 inch Quartet worth it?
faq.a: If you plan at the desk, yes. It is the only magnetic board with trays here, but it is also the only one in the $100 to $200 bucket, so smaller boards cost far less, and the magnets are the main reason to pay more.

faq.q: How do I clean a glass board?
faq.a: Follow the manufacturer's instructions. The listings do not state a method, so check the product page. Wipe soon after writing, and avoid abrasive pads on the glass, which can scratch it over time.

finalTake: Buy the Quartet GDP1723W if you plan on a real work surface, and the TSJ OFFICE if a small desk needs storage and a board in one. The GDP186 suits notes in front of a monitor. The smaller boards are fine for lists and trials, but they are not planning tools.
